title: The month of Assu
hookLine: in Assu love wells up: how can I meet the Lord (Barah Maha, ang 135)

lines: ASSU: THE RAINS END, THE SKY CLEARS.
BUT HOW DO I GET THERE?
cards: By Assu, roughly mid-September to mid-October in Punjab, the monsoon has usually blown itself out.
The mud dries, the nights cool, and the sky goes a hard, clear blue, the kind where you can suddenly see far hills that were hidden all summer.
Doubt is a lot like the rainy season: while it lasts, you can't see past the next puddle. Then one morning the air clears, and what's left isn't certainty. It's wanting.
You can see where you'd like to go, with no idea how to get there. That's exactly where Guru Arjan's Assu stanza begins.

teach.b: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: in Assu, love wells up. How can I go and meet the Lord? In Gurmukhi it begins asun prem umaahrraa.
Prem is love. Umaahrraa is eagerness, a surge that rises on its own.

teach.h: KIAU MILEE-AI: HOW CAN I MEET?
teach.b: Then the question that gives today its line: kiau milee-ai, how can I meet? Mind and body, the stanza says, are thirsty for a sight of the Beloved. And the bride does something very human.
She calls out: O mother, will someone come and bring me to Him? The Barah Maha doesn't scold her for asking. In the Sikh reading, the question is the first step.
Bhadon was confusion, attached to second things. Assu is the same person, now pointed in one direction, even without knowing the road. Then the stanza answers, gently.
The saints are the helpers of love, and she falls at their feet. In Sikh life that points to the sangat, the company of people also on the way, and to the Guru's word they sing together.
Without the Lord, the stanza asks, how can there be peace? There's no other place to go.
It closes on grace: in Assu, those live in peace on whom the Lord shows mercy.
So the answer to how isn't a technique. It's company, and longing, and a door opened from the other side. The not-knowing is allowed.

how: On the Sangrand that begins Assu, gurdwaras that keep the day read Guru Arjan's Assu stanza from the Barah Maha in Raag Majh, often with a short talk on its meaning for the month ahead.

o: the month a bride goes back to her mother's home
a harvest fair held when the rains end
the clear month when love asks how to meet

games.q: the month of Assu — tap the pairs.

s: the Assu stanza scolds the bride for not knowing the way
it lets her ask, then answers: the holy company helps, and mercy brings peace.
in the stanza, the bride turns to her mother for help
she calls out, O mother, will someone come and bring me to the Beloved?
the stanza's answer to how is a special technique
its answer is company, longing and grace.

games.q: the doubt has cleared and you want to meet the Beloved, but you don't know the way. what does the Assu stanza turn to?
o: wait alone until the longing fades.
the saints, the helpers of love.
a long journey to a faraway shrine.
games.why: the bride falls at the feet of the saints, love's helpers, and the stanza ends: those on whom the Lord shows mercy live in peace.

practice: Let your breathing slow and ask, honestly, what you long for underneath the to-do list: peace, closeness, forgiveness, a sense of being found.

If you pray, carry the stanza's own question on the breath, kiau milee-ai, how can I meet You; if you don't, just let the longing be there, without fixing or explaining it. Breathe in the wanting, and breathe out the hurry.

wordCard.voice: Assu. In Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, Assu is when love wells up and asks how to meet, and the stanza answers: through the holy company, and by mercy.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: prem, love. In Assu, the stanza says, prem wells up, umaahrraa, an eager surge.

carryVoice: Your line: assu: how to meet. Asking is already a step. That's day five hundred seventy-two.
